research_text:
# Research brief: `KeyPairGeneratorSpec`

## 1. API and finding

`java.security.KeyPairGenerator` creates public/private key pairs for a selected algorithm and associates algorithm-specific parameters with the keys. The reported message concerns the **`AlgorithmParameterSpec` value passed to an `initialize` overload**, not the generated `KeyPair` itself. Oracle describes that argument as the parameter set used to generate the keys. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))

The CrySL rule binds that argument as `params` and conditionally requires an algorithm-specific `prepared…[params]` predicate. Thus, the message is consistent with the analyzer not establishing the required preparation predicate. It does **not**, by itself, establish which algorithm or parameter values were used, whether Java would reject them, or whether a particular key size is invalid. The supplied finding is labeled `UnsatisfiedConstraint`; the rule source itself does not map that diagnostic label to a particular clause. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))

Sources:  
Oracle API: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html  
CrySL rule: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl

## 2. Documented usage and remediation

Oracle documents obtaining a generator with `getInstance`, initializing it either with a key size or an algorithm-specific parameter spec, and generating a pair. The overloads without an explicit `SecureRandom` obtain a randomness source as documented by the API. Oracle’s JCA guide illustrates algorithm-specific initialization with a `DSAParameterSpec` constructed from DSA parameters `p`, `q`, and `g`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))

A provider must document defaults for a generator that is not explicitly initialized. Oracle nevertheless **recommends explicit initialization**, because defaults can differ between providers and change across versions. An unsupported key size can cause `InvalidParameterException`; inappropriate parameter values can cause `InvalidAlgorithmParameterException`. A provider that does not implement parameter-spec initialization can throw `UnsupportedOperationException`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html?utm_source=openai))

Oracle does not prescribe a universal replacement parameter set or a remediation for this particular CrySL diagnostic. The appropriate documented parameters depend on the algorithm and provider; the rule’s predicate requirement is distinct from Java’s runtime API contract.

JCA guide: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html

## 3. Compatibility and migration

- **Persisted and wire formats:** Oracle documents `Key.getEncoded()` and `getFormat()`. Standard representations include X.509 `SubjectPublicKeyInfo` for public keys and PKCS#8 `PrivateKeyInfo` for private keys; a key can also report no encoding. `KeyFactory` can convert between compatible key specifications and key objects. These APIs do not guarantee that a consumer accepts a newly selected algorithm, parameter set, or key size. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/security/Key.html))
- **Platform support:** The parameter-spec overloads are documented since Java 1.2. Java SE 21 specifies minimum required algorithms and sizes, but additional support depends on the implementation and provider. For example, `ECGenParameterSpec` is documented since Java 1.5, and its supported names are provider-dependent. These statements do not establish support on an unspecified deployment platform. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html?utm_source=openai))
- **Migration path:** The cited generator documentation does not specify an automatic migration of stored keys or a wire-protocol migration for changed initialization. `KeyFactory` documents conversion of compatible representations, not conversion of an existing key into a newly generated key. `generateKeyPair()` generates a new pair on each call. Compatibility with existing consumers therefore remains an open question for the actual algorithm, provider, format, and protocol. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyFactory.html))

Key and key-factory documentation:  
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/security/Key.html  
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyFactory.html

## 4. Exact rule declaration and matching limits

The supplied rule source declares `SPEC java.security.KeyPairGenerator`. Its relevant initialization event clause is: ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))

```text
	i1: initialize(keysize);
	i2: initialize(keysize, _);
	i3: initialize(params);
	i4: initialize(params, _);
	Init := i1 | i2 | i3 | i4;
```

The source declares `keysize` as `int` and `params` as `java.security.spec.AlgorithmParameterSpec`. **Yes, the event declarations constrain the parameter list:** they distinguish one- and two-argument forms and bind the first argument as either `keysize` or `params`; the second argument is written `_`. The rule also declares one- and two-argument `getInstance` events and zero-argument `generateKeyPair` and `genKeyPair` events, with the order `Get, Init, Gen`. `getInstance` is a static factory; the initialization and generation events concern the specified generator type. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))

The rule then declares an algorithm allowlist, algorithm-dependent integer-size constraints, and conditional requirements for `preparedRSA`, `preparedDSA`, `preparedDH`, or `preparedEC` on `params`. It also declares the ensured `generatedKeypair` predicate. The source does not explain how a detector evaluates the `keysize` constraints when only a parameter spec is bound. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))

**A name alone is not the matching clause shown in this source:** the rule specifies `java.security.KeyPairGenerator` and event parameter forms, rather than declaring a name-only match for an unrelated receiver type. The source itself does not specify the detector’s complete method-resolution or subtype-matching implementation, so it cannot establish every case an analyzer version may match. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))

## Source limits and unresolved questions

The rule URL points to mutable `master`; the supplied SHA-256 and the rule-pack commit used for the finding were not independently verified. The detector version and analysis trace are also unavailable. Consequently, the exact diagnostic-to-clause mapping, resolved method, algorithm, provider, initialization values, predicate provenance, and generated-key consumers remain unresolved.
